American drivers line up for their ration of gasoline during the OPEC oil embargo crisis. 1974

I remember this. My babysitter was driving me home from school and we went to the gas station like any other day, but because of this, we unexpectedly got stuck in a line of cars that was several blocks long and it took us almost two hours to get gas and go home. Lots of people were angry and yelling and arguing.

The OPEC oil embargo was a response to American involvement in the 1973 Yom Kippur War. Six days after Egypt and Syria launched a surprise military campaign against Israel, the US supplied Israel with arms. In response to this, OPEC announced a reduction in production and an oil embargo against Canada, Japan, the Netherlands, the UK and the US. The price of oil quadrupled by 1974 to nearly US$12 per barrel. Control of oil became known as the "oil weapon."

US retail price gas prices rose from a national average of 38.5 cents in May 1973 to 55.1 cents in June 1974. Price controls were instituted nationally and states implemented various rationing systems. Odd–even rationing allowed vehicles with license plates having an odd number as the last digit to buy gas only on odd-numbered days of the month, while others could buy only on even-numbered days. In some states, a three-color flag system was used to denote gasoline availability at service stations—green for unrationed availability, yellow for restricted/rationed sales and red for out of stock. Many retailers chose not to sell gas on weekends. The national speed limit was also reduced to 55 mph and year-round daylight saving time was implemented from January 6, 1974, to February 23, 1975.

The embargo was lifted once the political demands of OPEC were met.
